bill.title: A bill to repeal certain Acts that impose sanctions upon Syria.
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 501.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would repeal certain laws that impose sanctions on Syria. The text does not specify which sanctions laws would be repealed or provide details about the scope of the changes. Without access to the full bill text, it is not possible to describe precisely what would change.

industries.rationale: Lifting Syria sanctions could affect oil and gas companies' ability to operate in or trade with Syrian energy markets.
Sanctions repeal would change banks' regulatory obligations regarding transactions with Syrian entities and individuals.
Removing sanctions could open Syrian markets to manufacturers currently restricted from exporting goods to Syria.
Sanctions relief could affect shipping and logistics companies' ability to conduct trade with Syrian ports and markets.

plain.whatItDoes: No one has written a summary of this bill yet. All we have is its title, and a title is not a description of a law. To find out what it does, you have to open the bill itself.
plain.whoItTouches: Mostly people outside the United States. It reaches most readers here only indirectly.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
